content: The Maternal and Child Health and Nutrition Division in the United States, represented by Kathleen Hill from JHPIEGO, a USAID grantee based in Washington, D.C., focuses on improving maternal and newborn health outcomes. Bo Jacobsson, a member of the FIGO Committee on Safe Motherhood and Newborn Health, is affiliated with the Department of Obstetrics at the University Medical Center Utrecht in the Netherlands. Jeffrey Smith, representing the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, and Gerry Visser, also from the FIGO Committee and the University Medical Center Utrecht, contribute to advancing maternal and newborn health initiatives. Charlotte Warren, from the Population Council in Washington, D.C., and Ingela Wiklund, part of the International Confederation of Midwifery Evidence Synthesis Group, are key contributors to maternal and newborn health research. Anna Cuthbert, an editor for the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group at the University of Liverpool, United Kingdom, plays a significant role in synthesizing evidence for maternal health guidelines. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued recommendations on the use of antiplatelet agents, particularly aspirin, for the prevention of pre-eclampsia. Aspirin, an irreversible cyclooxygenase inhibitor, reduces platelet aggregation by inhibiting the production of thromboxane A2. It also exhibits antipyretic, analgesic, and anti-inflammatory properties. The recommendations are based on evidence from a Cochrane systematic review, which included 77 randomized trials involving 40,249 women and their babies. These trials assessed the effects of antiplatelet agents for both primary and secondary prevention of pre-eclampsia. The systematic review categorized women by their level of risk for pre-eclampsia at trial entry: low risk (e.g., primiparity, family history of pre-eclampsia, age >40 years, or multiple pregnancy), moderate risk (two of the aforementioned factors), and high risk (e.g., diabetes, chronic hypertension, renal disease, autoimmune disease, positive uterine artery Doppler, previous history of pre-eclampsia, or previous fetal/neonatal death associated with pre-eclampsia). The timing of antiplatelet therapy initiation varied, with some trials starting therapy before 20 weeks of gestation and others at 20 weeks or later. Dosing regimens also varied, with aspirin doses ranging from less than 75 mg to 150 mg per day. The trials demonstrated that antiplatelet agents, particularly low-dose aspirin, are effective in reducing the risk of pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, and other adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. For primary prevention, women without gestational hypertension were recruited, while secondary prevention trials included women with gestational hypertension, intrauterine growth restriction, or both. The evidence supports the use of antiplatelet agents in women at risk of pre-eclampsia to improve maternal and perinatal outcomes. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of considering maternal risk factors, gestational age at therapy initiation, and aspirin dosage when implementing antiplatelet therapy for pre-eclampsia prevention. The recommendations aim to reduce maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality associated with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
